lead: Shear in an RC beam arrives as diagonal tension inside the web. Bending and shear act together; at the neutral axis the principal tensile stress equals the shear stress, acting at about 45° to the axis. Concrete is weak in tension, so a fine diagonal crack opens first. After that the beam stays up only because four things share the work: uncracked concrete above the crack, aggregate interlock, dowel action of the bars, and stirrups. Every shear rule in IS 456 comes from this picture.
prereq: You need Unit 1 for characteristic strength and partial safety factors, Unit 2 for the singly reinforced section and effective depth; stirrup design continues in 3.2 Design of shear reinforcement.

blocks.text: A beam section carries two stresses at once. Bending gives a horizontal stress σ, compression on top and tension at the bottom. Shear force V gives a shear stress τ, equal on horizontal and vertical planes. Combined, they produce a principal tensile stress inclined to the axis.

blocks.where: σ₁ is the principal tensile stress at a point (MPa); σ is the bending stress there, positive in compression (MPa), so compression on top makes σ positive and the term −σ/2 reduces the tension; τ is the shear stress from τ = VQ/(Ib) (MPa); V is the shear force at the section (N); Q is the first moment of area of the part above the point about the neutral axis (mm³); I is the second moment of area (mm⁴); b is the width at that point (mm).

blocks.text: At the neutral axis σ = 0, so σ₁ = τ. This peak tension acts on a plane at 45° to the beam axis: diagonal tension. Concrete cracks when the principal tension passes its direct tensile strength, roughly 10% of f_ck.

Near the support the bending moment is small, so the crack is steep: a web-shear crack. Where the moment is also large, an existing flexural crack bends over into the diagonal: a flexure-shear crack. Both are diagonal tension.

sections.h3: Four things carry the shear after cracking

blocks.text: An unreinforced beam splits and drops as soon as the first diagonal crack opens. A reinforced beam survives because four mechanisms take the shear.

items: Uncracked concrete above the diagonal crack: the compression zone stays whole and carries roughly 20 to 40% of the shear, acting as the chord of a truss.
Aggregate interlock: the two rough faces of a narrow crack rub and pass shear as friction. It works only while the crack is narrow, roughly under 0.3 mm.
Dowel action: the longitudinal bars crossing the crack act as pins and transfer shear by bending locally. Bar yielding or splitting along the bars kills it.
Stirrups: vertical or inclined steel crosses the crack and takes tension directly. Before cracking it does little; after cracking it is the only dependable part.

blocks.text: The truss analogy assembles these parts. The compression zone is the top chord, the tension steel is the bottom chord, the concrete between diagonal cracks is a set of struts at about 45°, and the stirrups are vertical ties. Load travels down the struts and up the ties, so the beam behaves like a truss with a cracked web.

A stirrup works best when it crosses a crack at right angles. A vertical stirrup meets a 45° crack at 45°, so only the component of its tension acting across the crack, T sin 45° ≈ 0.707 T, resists the crack, where T is the stirrup tension in N. An inclined stirrup at 45° crosses the crack at 90°, all of its tension acts across the crack, and it is √2 times as effective for the same area. The design formula is in 3.2.

sections.h3: Failure modes, τ_v, τ_c and the critical section

items: Diagonal tension (web shear) failure: a sudden diagonal crack splits the web where no stirrup crosses it. Brittle, no warning.
Shear-compression failure: the diagonal crack grows into the compression zone above the support or under the load, and concrete crushes after the stirrups yield. This one gives warning.
Web crushing: the diagonal strut crushes in a thin web under heavy shear. Widening the web or raising the concrete grade is the only cure; extra stirrups do not help.

blocks.where: τ_v is the nominal shear stress (N/mm², that is MPa); V_u is the factored shear force at the section (N); b_w is the width of the web (mm), equal to the full width b for a rectangular beam; d is the effective depth (mm).

blocks.text: The concrete's own share is τ_c, read from IS 456 Table 19. It rises with concrete grade and with p_t = 100 A_st/(b_w d), the percentage of tension steel, where A_st is the area of tension steel in mm². More steel means a stiffer section, a narrower crack and better aggregate interlock. For M25 with p_t ≈ 0.9%, τ_c = 0.62 MPa, interpolated from Table 19.

The upper limit τ_c,max depends only on the grade: 2.8 MPa for M20, 3.1 MPa for M25, 3.5 MPa for M30. Three checks follow. If τ_v ≤ τ_c, minimum stirrups are enough. If τ_c < τ_v ≤ τ_c,max, design stirrups for V_us = (τ_v − τ_c) b_w d, where V_us is the shear carried by the shear reinforcement in N. If τ_v > τ_c,max, enlarge the section or raise the concrete grade.

The shear used is not the reaction at the support, but the shear at the critical section, a distance d from the face of the support. Closer than that, the load arches directly into the support through a short concrete strut, the full diagonal crack cannot form, and the shear there is not critical.

figure.caption: The factored shear opens a diagonal crack; the beam then carries that shear through the uncracked compression zone, aggregate interlock, dowel action and stirrups.

spec.aria: A shear load opens a diagonal crack; the beam then carries it by concrete compression, aggregate interlock, dowel action and stirrups.

examples.question: A rectangular RC beam has width b = 300 mm, overall depth D = 600 mm and effective depth d = 550 mm. The tension steel is A_st = 1485 mm², so p_t = 100 × 1485/165,000 = 0.9%. The factored shear at the critical section is V_u = 180 kN. Concrete is M25, with design shear strength τ_c = 0.62 MPa and maximum shear stress τ_c,max = 3.1 MPa. Find τ_v and state whether shear reinforcement is required.
steps: Write the data: b_w = 300 mm, d = 550 mm, V_u = 180 kN, τ_c = 0.62 MPa, τ_c,max = 3.1 MPa.
Convert the shear to newtons: V_u = 180 × 10³ = 180,000 N.
Compute the concrete area resisting shear: b_w d = 300 × 550 = 165,000 mm².
Nominal shear stress: τ_v = V_u/(b_w d) = 180,000/165,000 = 1.0909 MPa, about 1.09 MPa.
Compare with the concrete strength: τ_c = 0.62 MPa < τ_v = 1.09 MPa, so concrete alone cannot carry the shear and stirrups are needed.
Compare with the upper limit: τ_v = 1.09 MPa < τ_c,max = 3.1 MPa, so the web will not crush and the section size is kept.
Shear to be carried by the stirrups: V_us = (τ_v − τ_c) b_w d = (1.0909 − 0.62) × 165,000 = 77,700 N = 77.7 kN, using the unrounded τ_v.
examples.answer: τ_v = 1.09 MPa; since 0.62 < 1.09 < 3.1 MPa, the section is safe against web crushing but concrete alone is not enough, so vertical stirrups must carry V_us = 77.7 kN.
examples.check:
b_w = 300.0
d = 550.0
V_u = 180e3
tau_c = 0.62
tau_v = V_u / (b_w * d)
print(round(tau_v, 2))
V_us = (tau_v - tau_c) * b_w * d / 1000.0
print(round(V_us, 1))

traps: Using the maximum shear at the support face instead of V_u at the critical section, d away. This over-designs and loses marks.
Treating τ_c as fixed. It depends on concrete grade and p_t = 100 A_st/(b_w d); the same M25 section gives a different τ_c when the tension steel changes.
Mixing units: with V_u in kN, τ_v = V_u × 10³/(b_w d) in N/mm². Forgetting 10³ gives an answer 1000 times too small.
Thinking τ_c,max is added to τ_c, or that more stirrups rescue a section with τ_v > τ_c,max. Beyond τ_c,max only a bigger section or a higher grade helps.
Using overall depth D instead of effective depth d in τ_v = V_u/(b_w d).

quiz.q: Define diagonal tension in an RC beam.
quiz.a: The principal tensile stress at the neutral axis, where σ = 0 and σ₁ = τ, acting at about 45° to the beam axis.

quiz.q: Why is the critical section for shear taken at a distance d from the face of the support and not at the support itself?
quiz.a: Within distance d the load arches directly into the support through a short concrete strut. The full diagonal crack cannot form there, so the support-face shear overstates the real demand.

quiz.q: Why does τ_c increase as the percentage of tension steel increases?
quiz.a: More tension steel stiffens the section and narrows the diagonal crack, keeping aggregate interlock and dowel action working, so the concrete carries more shear.

quiz.q: A beam has b_w = 250 mm, d = 450 mm and V_u = 120 kN at the critical section. Find τ_v.
For that beam, τ_c = 0.56 MPa and τ_c,max = 3.1 MPa. What do you provide?
quiz.a: τ_c < τ_v < τ_c,max, so keep the section and design stirrups for V_us = (1.07 − 0.56) × 250 × 450 = 57,375 N ≈ 57.4 kN.

quiz.q: Why do extra stirrups not prevent web crushing failure?
quiz.a: Web crushing is failure of the diagonal concrete strut itself. Stirrups control tension across the crack; they cannot raise the compressive strength of the strut, so only a thicker web or a higher grade helps.

quiz.q: A stirrup inclined at 45° is more effective than a vertical one of the same area. Explain using the crack direction.
quiz.a: The crack is at about 45°. A vertical stirrup crosses it at 45° and only 0.707 of its tension acts across the crack. An inclined stirrup at 45° crosses the crack at 90° and all of its tension acts across it, so it is √2 times as effective.

beyond: Not for the exam. Shear gives the least warning of the limit states, so checking existing bridges often uses nonlinear finite element analysis with cracked concrete models rather than a single τ_c. Deep beams, pile caps and corbels fall outside beam theory and use strut-and-tie models, which extend the truss analogy. Fibre-reinforced concrete improves aggregate interlock. For deeper reading search strut-and-tie modelling, critical shear crack theory, and shear in prestressed sections in Unit 6.
